aspects.says: Thread.ofVirtual(), Thread.startVirtualThread and the per-task executors create virtual threads, which are always daemon and NORM_PRIORITY.
aspects.reason: lookup detail in the reference table; unit 6.1.1 and its practices already cover naming and daemon status, and every practice here runs on these APIs

aspects.says: On Java 21 a virtual thread that blocks inside synchronized or a native method keeps its carrier; JDK 24 removed the synchronized case.
basis: section:A Virtual Thread That Waits Gives Its Carrier Back, So a Few Platform Threads Run Thousands of Requests
aspects.reason: behaviour that differs between Java 21 and the Java 25 runner, so no graded test may depend on it; the page states it as a side note and unit 6.7.2 covers it

aspects.says: A virtual thread that computes without blocking keeps its carrier until it blocks or ends, so long CPU work on virtual threads delays every other virtual thread.
basis: section:A Virtual Thread That Computes Keeps Its Carrier: Java 21 Has No Time Slice

aspects.says: CPU-heavy work goes to a platform pool sized to the cores, and the virtual thread waits for its result, which frees the carrier.
basis: section:A Virtual Thread That Computes Keeps Its Carrier: Java 21 Has No Time Slice

aspects.says: The expensive, non-thread-safe object is pooled with a bound, borrowed per task and given back on every path, while each task keeps its own virtual thread.
basis: section:One Thread per Task Means Nothing Per-Thread Is Reused: Pool the Expensive Object, Not the Thread

aspects.says: A waiting virtual thread keeps its frames, and every object they reference, on the heap, so memory grows with the requests in flight and must be limited where requests enter.
basis: section:A Waiting Virtual Thread Keeps Its Stack, and Everything It References, on the Heap

aspects.says: With a thread per task a ThreadLocal value is built for each task, and pooling virtual threads to get the cache back brings back the pool's limit.
basis: section:One Thread per Task Means Nothing Per-Thread Is Reused: Pool the Expensive Object, Not the Thread

aspects.says: A virtual thread that blocks in a JDK call is unmounted and its carrier runs other virtual threads, so a few carriers serve thousands of waiting requests.
basis: section:A Virtual Thread That Waits Gives Its Carrier Back, So a Few Platform Threads Run Thousands of Requests
